data.name: WRC 5 FIA World Rally Championship
data.detailed_description:
WRC 5: a melhor simulação de rali.


Encontra todos os carros, pilotos e ralis oficiais do Campeonato Mundial de Rali 2015 da FIA no novo padrão de qualidade dos simuladores de corridas. Sente o impacto das diferentes superfícies no comportamento do teu carro graças a um novo motor de física que recria de forma fiel as sensações de conduzir em gravilha, neve, asfalto, terra, gelo e areia. Vive o espírito dos 13 ralis espalhados pelo mundo! Conduz de noite e de dia sob sol, chuva e neve.
Aprende as bases da condução com o novo modo Escola de Rali, aperfeiçoa as tuas habilidades no modo Carreira, personaliza as definições, compete contra outros pilotos online e torna-te um verdadeiro campeão de rali!

reviews.review:
[h3]A Game With Caveats[/h3]
As a long-time DiRT Rally player, I initially played in cockpit view and enabled the simulation setting, which by default disables all driving assists, enables manual transmission and sets car damage to high. It took me many races in Junior WRC and WRC 2 to realize cockpit view and high car damage are bad ideas. The game only feels nice to drive in front camera view with medium car damage. I learned this the hard way after falling into these two pits. 

[h3]The Visibility (and Pace Note) Problem[/h3]
Rainy and night stages are new additions to WRC 5, but like dusk stages, they suffer from poor visibility because headlights are too dim. The short draw distance compounds the issue, as objects often pop in just before you reach them. 

With high car damage, things get even worse in cockpit view, because the windshield quickly gets covered in dirt and stains, blocking your vision. WRC 4 has the same problem, yet visibility only gets bad when the car is damaged. WRC 5 is worse since windshield gets dirty without damage. As you have no control over the wiper to clean the windshield, it is difficult to see and react quickly to what's ahead. 

There is also a bizarre issue I encountered while driving the Hyundai i20 for WRC. After a few events, I felt like either my seat sank lower, or the dash became higher, because I could barely see the road ahead in cockpit view. That’s when I realize front camera view is the GOAT, and more on that later.

Pace notes should help with visibility, but reading the note is such a mess. Instead of reading instructions before each corner, no matter what setting I use, co-driver just blasts through several instructions all at once. As a result, pace notes are practically useless, forcing players to rely on quick reactions and on-screen prompts.

[h3]The High Car Damage (and Junior WRC) Problem[/h3]
I think the problem is that high car damage comes with excessive car degradation and damage, like the dirty windshield is caused by cleanness degrading or something. Brake and tires also wear out way too fast, causing handling to feel inconsistent. Worse, suspension seems to have sharp degradation. You can drive safely with four suspensions in good condition, then suddenly start to hear suspensions constantly buttoning out, even on a flat road. Shortly after, all four suspensions are completely wrecked, which feels so frustrating and unfair– just how suspensions blow themselves up?

Not just the degradation, car damage itself is all over the place, too. It is quite funny that going over a few bumps fast and hard can fry your radio from electronic damage, then no pace note reading for you, not that it is helpful anyway. Suspension damage is the worst because it severely impedes controlling the car, and it is wildly unpredictable (damage caused by players not degradation). Flying over a crest is sometimes fine, and sometimes damages the suspension, and sometimes suspension is so fragile that it is damaged from some unevenness at the roadside you tend to ignore. 

Junior WRC is still the worst career tier, but for a different reason than the lack of speed in WRC 4 (last game). You can only drive the Citroën DS3 that can’t be tuned, but its gear ratios are so terribly short that the first two gear hit redline almost instantly. 

With simulation setting enabled (manual transmission and high car damage), and since human don’t shift as instantaneous as automatic transmission, I had to launch the car in third gear, which made me suspect Junior WRC wasn’t designed with manual shift in mind.

Short gear ratios also make gearbox easy to break because players often can’t shift fast enough to keep up with the engine redline, especially if you also hit something during the race, which is very common. Then you’re stuck in third gear until it is fixed. With high car damage, cars really feel like cardboard boxes that just keep breaking and falling apart.

[h3]How You Play the Game Matters[/h3]
Fortunately, the game lets you adjust car damage separately. I switched to medium car damage for WRC and immediately felt much better. Brake and tire degradation are still exaggerated compared to real life, but overall, damage is much more manageable, and cars also handle more consistently.

I tested out all the camera views when I had issue with cockpit view in the Hyundai. Turned out front camera provides a far superior feel of driving compared to others. It has a proper sense of speed so that you can find braking points accurately and reliably. You can tell what direction the front wheels are heading and when rear wheels are gripping or starting to slide. The chassis weight shift also feels so direct, swift and clear. Whereas in other views, feedback from the cars is vague: you don’t feel the car is fast, you don’t know what the front axis is doing, the weight shift feels slow and clunky and by the time you realize the rear is sliding, usually you are already spinning out.

[h3]What’s Improved since WRC 4 [/h3]
WRC 5 was released in 2015, two years after WRC 4. It is not like it doesn’t have improvements. The online servers are still up (online achievements obtainable), though you can’t match anyone, and you don’t have to fiddle with game files to get it running properly on modern hardware. However, the game may often look forzen because confirmation screens don’t always show up, such as when exiting the game or confirming which car components to repair. It is probably caused by the menu running at over 1000 FPS. You just need to know there is a confirmation screen that doesn’t appear waiting for your input.

Beyond the usual visuals update, the cars sound less terrible (some still sound like aggressive vacuum cleaners), but the epic background music is gone. WRC 5 has a rally school teaching newcomers basic but useful rally knowledge, though it's pretty stupid that you have to follow the exact driving line to pass each practice session. What stands out most is that service intervals now vary between one, two, or three stages instead of a fixed two, which adds a welcome challenge in keeping your car intact.

My biggest criticism of WRC 4 is that cars decelerate automatically when you simply lift off the throttle and turn the wheel, which is no longer the case here. With all driving assists off, WRC 5 feels closer to an arcade-sim, since the handling doesn’t feel heavily assisted, even though the cars seem to have more understeer than the previous game. 

Another improvement is that road surfaces feel more distinct to drive on. You can at least feel the reduced grip on snow and wet roads, whereas in WRC 4, different surfaces feel pretty much the same. However, physics is not entirely convincing. Once you drive off the road, the car loses momentum unnaturally, and far more dramatically than it should, as if some kind of automatic deceleration has kicked in.

[h3]Verdict[/h3]
I did find the setting that makes WRC 5 fun, and the game does improve on the predecessor in some ways, but there are just many things the game does bad that had me fighting it for a big chunk of my playtime. And even without those caveats, the experience is quite average. With all the games in the series being dirt cheap right now, I don’t find this one particularly worthwhile.
